name: Ginseng root extract

lead: Ginseng root extract comes from Panax ginseng, a root central to East Asian traditional medicine. In skincare it shows up in K-beauty and herbal products, used for a fresher, healthier, more youthful look.

The chain proponents describe is antioxidant: ginsenosides in the root reduced inflammatory and oxidative signalling in cell and animal studies, which maps to less oxidative stress in skin. Most published research is on oral ginseng for general health, where systematic reviews found efficacy could not be established; no clinical trial of topical use for appearance was found.

paras: Used in creams, essences, serums and herbal soaps as an antioxidant or soothing botanical, usually within a wider anti-aging routine with sunscreen and moisturiser. Some people also take it orally as a supplement. Users describe cumulative, gradual changes over weeks of use.

Oral ginseng has reported side effects, including headache, insomnia and raised blood pressure, and interacts with drugs such as warfarin. Topical products carry standard external-use and irritation warnings.

angle.text: Ginseng root extract is used in K-beauty and herbal skincare as an antioxidant that gives skin a healthier, more youthful look. Ginsenosides lowered oxidative and inflammatory signalling in cell and animal studies, and the research on ginseng is mostly about oral use.

lead: Ginseng root extract is a preparation made from the root of Panax ginseng, a perennial herb native to mountainous parts of Korea, northeast China and the Russian Far East that has long been used in East Asian folk medicine.[1][1] In skincare it is used as an ingredient in K-beauty and herbal products, where it is marketed mainly as an antioxidant or soothing botanical; one US-listed topical product containing it is a herbal medicated soap.[2]

Most of the published research concerns oral ginseng for general health claims rather than topical use for appearance. Systematic reviews of randomised trials concluded that the efficacy of ginseng root extract could not be established beyond doubt for any indication studied, and laboratory studies have reported anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in cells and animals.[3][4][3] No clinical trial of topical ginseng root extract for skin appearance appears among the sources reviewed.

paras: In cosmetics, ginseng root extract appears in creams, essences and soaps, usually described by brands as antioxidant, revitalising or soothing. A DailyMed-listed topical herbal soap lists Panax ginseng root extract as an ingredient and carries standard external-use warnings: keep out of eyes and stop use if irritation occurs.[2]
Outside cosmetics, ginseng is taken orally for vitality, immune function, cognition, cardiovascular health and sexual function, according to a review of adverse effects.[3]

Ginsenosides and other phytochemicals in the root are the compounds most often studied. A 2022 laboratory and animal study reported that a ginseng root extract reduced inflammatory signalling (MAPK/NF-kB) and activated antioxidant pathways (Nrf2-Keap1) in cultured cells and in a mouse colitis model.[5] These findings come from non-skin models and do not directly test topical appearance effects.

Other laboratory work has examined ginsenoside conversion by microbial enzymes and the use of ginseng extract to synthesise metal nanoparticles; these concern chemistry and materials rather than cosmetic use.

Wikipedia notes that ginseng is generally considered safe for adults for under six months, with possible drug interactions (for example with warfarin) and common side effects including headache, insomnia, raised blood pressure, diarrhoea and skin rash.[1] A systematic review of adverse effects and interactions reached similar conclusions about the oral herb.[3] The product label for the soap advises external use only.[2]

No clinical studies of ginseng root extract applied to the skin for appearance were found. Human trials of oral ginseng exist for other outcomes. A 1999 systematic review of double-blind randomised trials found the evidence for efficacy of ginseng root extract inconclusive across indications.[4] A randomised trial in overweight and obese people with impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes found that ginseng and ginsenoside Re did not improve beta-cell function or insulin sensitivity.[6] Registered trials have examined ginseng extracts for cognition, fatigue, bone metabolism in menopausal women and exercise performance.[7][8]

timeline.event: Jesuit Pierre Jartoux writes a letter describing ginseng, published in 1713.[1]
A systematic review of randomised trials finds the efficacy of ginseng root extract not established.[4]
A systematic review catalogues adverse effects and drug interactions of Panax ginseng.[3]
